purpose: Febuxostat is used to lower high levels of uric acid in the blood, a condition called hyperuricemia. It is mainly prescribed for people who have gout, which is a painful type of arthritis caused by uric acid crystals building up in the joints. By keeping uric acid levels low, it helps prevent future gout attacks.
how_it_works: Your body naturally produces uric acid when it breaks down certain substances called purines, found in foods and your own cells. Febuxostat blocks an enzyme called xanthine oxidase, which is the key enzyme your body uses to make uric acid. By blocking this enzyme, the drug lowers the amount of uric acid produced, so less of it builds up in your blood and joints.
common_side_effects: Some common side effects include nausea, joint pain or stiffness, rash, and mild swelling. You might actually notice more gout flare-ups when you first start this medicine — this is normal and does not mean the medicine is not working. Your doctor may give you another medication to help manage these early flares.
warnings: Important: Febuxostat has a boxed warning because studies showed a higher risk of heart-related death compared to another gout medicine called allopurinol, especially in people who already have heart disease. Tell your doctor if you have had a heart attack or stroke. Also call your doctor right away if you develop a serious rash, yellowing of the skin or eyes, or signs of an allergic reaction. Do not use this medicine if you also take certain chemotherapy drugs like azathioprine or mercaptopurine, as it can cause dangerous interactions.
typical_dosing: The usual starting dose is 40 mg taken by mouth once a day. If your uric acid level is still too high after a few weeks, your doctor may increase the dose to 80 mg once daily. You can take it with or without food, and try to take it at the same time each day to help you remember.
